Mini Project 1

Your choice of option, what each one asks for, the due date and how it is graded are on the Mini Project 1 page of the course site, linked from the calendar. This notebook is the shape to build it in. Keep the headings, and replace each line in italics with your own. Save it in your course repository as projects/mp1/<your-tool>.py, named for what it does, such as loan-schedule.py, and open it with uv run marimo edit.

1. The Question

Who would use this, and what decision does it help them make? Two or three sentences, in words somebody outside this course would understand.

Reorder simulation can be used by any small business owner / warehouse / inventory managers with a simple supply chain / stock flow that has any cost associated with holding, ordering, or stockouts of inventory. It helps determine stock ROP (Reorder Point) based on demand variability, lead time, and desired service level if applicable.

2. My Plan Before AI

Before you ask your agent anything, write how you would solve it: the steps, in order, in plain words, in five lines or more. Then answer these two questions:
  • What does your loop carry from one step to the next, the way a running total carries its sum?
  • Which check will you use in section 6, and which two numbers should agree?
Commit this notebook with the message mp1: plan before AI.

steps
  1. Declare list of reorder_points = [20, 30, 40, 50].
  2. For each reorder point:
  • Set inventory = 60.
  • Create an empty list of outstanding orders (orders placed but not yet delivered).
  • Create variables/lists to track lost sales, orders placed, ending stock, etc.
  1. For each day:
  • Check whether any order is due to arrive today. If yes, add it to inventory and remove it from outstanding orders.
  • Record the day's starting inventory.
  1. Process demand:
  • If inventory is at least demand, sell all demand.
  • Else, sell all remaining inventory, set inventory to 0, and record the unmet demand as lost sales.
  1. Calculate ending inventory.
  2. inventory position = ending inventory + all outstanding orders.
  3. If inventory position is less than or equal to the reorder point: Place an order for 100 cartons. Schedule it to arrive 3 days later. Save the day's results.
  4. Move to the next day, carrying forward the updated inventory and outstanding orders.
  5. After 30 days, calculate total units lost, days with lost sales, number of orders placed, and average ending inventory.

1. What does your loop carry from one step to the next, the way a running total carries its sum?
The loop
  • Carries the current inventory level and any outstanding orders that have been placed but not yet delivered.
  • Updates running totals of lost sales, orders placed, and ending inventory as it moves from one day to the next.
  1. Which check will you use in section 6, and which two numbers should agree?
Total Demand = Total Sold + Total Lost Sales

data.text/markdown: A reorder point of 40 is recommended: it is the lowest reorder point that avoids any lost sales (0 units lost over 30 days), while carrying less average stock (48.4 units) than reorder point 50 (58.4 units), which has the same zero lost sales.

data.text/markdown:
Comparing the two approaches The formula-based approach (Approach 1) gives a reorder point between 50 and 62, depending on how much safety stock (service level) you choose — 90% service level gives ROP ≈ 50, while 99.9% gives ROP ≈ 62. None of these are guaranteed to reach exactly zero lost sales, because the formula assumes demand follows a smooth bell curve and asks "how safe do you want to be," rather than looking at what actually happened in this specific dataset. The search approach (Approach 2) finds the exact answer for this dataset: a reorder point of 55 is the smallest one that gives zero lost sales over all 365 days. This lines up well with the formula's 99% service level estimate (57.0), but it is not a guess, it is the real smallest number that works for this exact year of demand. So reorder point 40 (the original heuristic) was too low once a full year of noisier demand was simulated — it is closer to Approach 1's 90% service level estimate (50.1) than to the exact zero-lost-sales answer (55). additional note:
  • method 1 is more standardized and scalable but fits more to clients with some statistics background knowledge to truely understand the choice we're trying to make.
  • adding more proper cost data (holding, ordering, sales lost) should give even more accurate optimization if data is available
